To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the four monitoring procedures were equally effective in improving oral reading rate and (2) teacher monitoring was preferred to self- and peer monitoring.
teacher-, peer-, and self-monitoring were equally effective in improving the oral reading rate for students with learning disabilities, but self-monitoring was the most effective.

(a) the teacher, peer, or self-monitoring conditions did not result in significantly different rates of improvement, but (b) students who monitored themselves improved at a faster rate than those who received teacher feedback.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of different methods of progress monitoring on the oral reading of elementary-age students with reading difficulties.
the effects of four forms of monitoring on the oral reading performance of students with learning disabilities.
the use of curriculum-based measurement to monitor the oral reading rate (i.e., number of correct words read per minute) of students with learning disabilities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-monitoring is a viable alternative for progress monitoring in special education classrooms.
teacher monitoring is a reliable and effective means of monitoring the progress of students with learning disabilities in the area of oral reading fluency.
self- and peer-monitored students were able to accurately collect and report oral reading data, and that self-monitoring may have the added benefit of improving students' performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of peer- and/or self-monitoring in conjunction with teacher monitoring may be beneficial in reducing the time special education teachers spend collecting data.
the use of peer- and teacher-monitoring in the classroom can be an effective means of collecting reliable and valid data on the oral reading fluency of students with learning disabilities.
the teacher-monitoring condition was superior to the self-monitoring condition in terms of reliability of the data and the number of correct responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
peer- and self-monitored progress monitoring is feasible and acceptable to students with learning disabilities and may provide an efficient way to collect reliable data on reading rate.
self-monitoring is a promising strategy for improving the academic performance of students with learning disabilities.
self- and peer- monitoring can be a useful alternative to teacher-monitoring for some students with learning disabilities.
